interactions: Ibuprofen with dexamethasone: additive risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding; ibuprofen also impairs platelet function. Avoid the combination.
Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin uptake and add to NSAID-related bleeding risk.
Sertraline with levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic interaction. Levetiracetam can cause irritability, low mood and, rarely, suicidal ideation; monitor mood in a patient treated for depression.
Levothyroxine with dexamethasone: glucocorticoids can lower TSH; dose change is not usually needed, recheck thyroid function if treatment is prolonged.
Lisinopril with dexamethasone: corticosteroids can raise blood pressure through fluid retention; monitor blood pressure.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Irregular heterogeneously enhancing left temporal mass (3.8 cm) with thick nodular enhancement and no central necrosis, restricted diffusion along the enhancing margins, vasogenic oedema, 2 mm midline shift and insular extension
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium (tumour protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterise the left temporal lesion, define mass effect and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion and FLAIR is the standard imaging for a suspected diffuse glioma: it defines the enhancing target, the oedema and the mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio 2.8 in the enhancing component, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and the sampling target
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion (DSC) to assess tumour vascularity and target the most aggressive region for tissue sampling
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the region to sample; it does not grade or exclude, tissue decides (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA 5.3 with lipid-lactate in the enhancing mass; mildly raised choline in the peritumoral zone
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterise the metabolic profile of the lesion
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated choline with reduced NAA and lipid-lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not establish the diagnosis, tissue does (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.label: Order CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast if a solitary metastasis remains on the differential
action_criteria.rationale: Staging for an extracranial primary is optional when the imaging favours a primary glioma and there is no history of cancer.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 134 mEq/L and glucose 105 mg/dL, mildly abnormal; normal counts and coagulation, type and screen done: no contraindication to surgery
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory work-up: CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT) and type and screen before neurosurgery
action_criteria.rationale: A neurosurgical procedure and corticosteroids are anticipated; platelets, coagulation, electrolytes and glucose must be known before either.

action_criteria.rationale: The choice between standard and hypofractionated treatment after the integrated diagnosis turns on age and KPS, with KPS under 70 the unfavourable threshold (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left language dominance (laterality index 0.72); displaced Wernicke activation about 8 mm from the tumour
action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI to map language and motor cortex relative to the lesion before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The lesion lies close to Wernicke area in the dominant hemisphere; functional mapping plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Arcuate fasciculus deviated but continuous, about 5 mm from the margin; Meyer loop in the temporal-stem oedema
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the arcuate fasciculus and optic radiation before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The lesion and its oedema lie close to the left arcuate fasciculus and Meyer loop; tractography plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H negative, IDH1/IDH2 wildtype on sequencing, ATRX retained and MGMT promoter unmethylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left temporal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.rationale: Dexamethasone and levetiracetam will be started; the current medicines and allergy are checked before prescribing.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the left temporal mass causes midline shift and temporal horn effacement, and the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not start radiotherapy, temozolomide or other tumour-directed therapy before the integrated tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given the planned neurosurgery and bleeding risk.
Do not use enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which interact with dexamethasone and temozolomide.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left temporal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Start antiseizure treatment with levetiracetam for the documented focal clonic seizure of the right hand; this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.
Stop as-needed ibuprofen before neurosurgery and while on dexamethasone (platelet inhibition and gastrointestinal bleeding risk, increased by sertraline); use paracetamol for headache.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 47 with KPS 80, the standard is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021); with an unmethylated MGMT promoter the benefit of temozolomide is smaller, so clinical trial options should also be discussed.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jerome Harris is a 47-year-old right-handed man and high school English teacher who presents with a 2-month history of progressive cognitive and behavioral changes, initially attributed to stress and worsening depression. His husband first noticed something was wrong approximately 8 weeks ago when he began struggling to find words during conversations, occasionally substituting incorrect words or trailing off mid-sentence. As an English teacher, his vocabulary had always been exceptional, and these lapses were immediately noticeable to family and colleagues. Over the following weeks, he became increasingly irritable and short-tempered, which was uncharacteristic. He snapped at students in class on several occasions and had two arguments with colleagues over trivial matters, prompting the principal to suggest he take a leave of absence. His husband also reports that he has become somewhat apathetic, losing interest in reading novels — previously his greatest passion — and spending hours staring at the television without engaging with the content. Approximately 6 weeks ago, he began complaining of dull, pressure-like headaches, predominantly on the left side, that were worse in the morning and would gradually improve over the course of the day. The headaches were initially responsive to ibuprofen but have become more persistent over the past 3 weeks. Three weeks ago, he had an episode where his right hand began shaking involuntarily for approximately 30 seconds while he was eating breakfast. He did not lose consciousness but felt confused for several minutes afterward. His husband witnessed the episode and described rhythmic jerking of the right hand that he could not suppress. He was evaluated by his primary care physician, who increased his sertraline dose, suspecting worsening depression. However, his symptoms continued to progress, and he was referred to neurology. At the outpatient neurology visit one week ago, the examining neurologist was concerned by his word-finding difficulty and subtle right-sided motor signs, and obtained an urgent non-contrast CT of the head, which showed a left temporal hypodensity with surrounding oedema; he was admitted for further workup. The patient himself acknowledges feeling 'not right' but minimizes the extent of his symptoms. He attributes his personality changes to stress at work and denies feeling depressed, though he admits he has been sleeping more than usual and has lost approximately 4 kg over the past two months without trying.
